title: Backyard Bible Study
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
QID: 14714_backyard_bible_study

Paul hosted a weekly backyard Bible-study cookout at his home. For several weeks, neighborhood youths had been stealing folding chairs from his personal patio after the gatherings. To catch them, Paul stayed awake each night watching the yard.

One evening Paul heard rustling near the back fence. He shouted for anyone there to leave. Receiving no answer, Paul fired a shotgun loaded with nonlethal buckshot into shrubs along the fence where he believed the youths might be hiding. Six-year-old Ruth was hiding in the shrubs and was struck in one eye by pellets, causing loss of sight.

If Paul is charged with second-degree assault, which is defined in the jurisdiction as “maliciously causing serious physical injury to another,” Paul is:

Source row used: BARMATRIX Q#14714, Criminal Law / Other Crimes, with C as the official key and the official explanation that malice may be implied from gross recklessness when the actor fires into bushes where he believes people may be hiding.  The prompt also required a Christian-first transformation, exact rule preservation, honest pick-rate provenance, and Gold/Silver Key treatment when anchor-dependent.  The reasoning posture file emphasizes naming the pivot and preserving the ambitious goal while policing unsupported claims.
call: If Paul is charged with second-degree assault, defined as maliciously causing serious physical injury to another, Paul is:

choices.A: not guilty, because Ruth was trespassing and Paul was using what he believed was nondeadly force.
choices.B: not guilty, because Paul did not intend to kill or to cause serious physical injury.
choices.C: guilty, because Paul recklessly caused serious physical injury.
choices.D: guilty, because there is no privilege to use force against a person who is too young to be criminally responsible.

rightExplanation: C is correct. Gold Key: “Maliciously” is not limited to a specific intent to kill or maim. It can be satisfied by extreme recklessness toward human life or serious injury. Silver Key: When the array gives B “no intent” and C “recklessly caused serious injury,” name the axis as intent-only malice vs reckless malice. The stem gives reckless firing into a place where Paul believed people might be hiding, plus loss of sight. That combination makes C the true-and-responsive answer.

wrongExplanations.A: It tries to move the case into a trespass/property-defense frame. The call defines the charged crime as maliciously causing serious physical injury. Trespass and Paul’s label of the force as “nondeadly” do not, by themselves, defeat the malice-and-injury charge.
wrongExplanations.B: Gold Key: malice does not require proof that Paul specifically intended to kill or cause serious physical injury. B treats lack of specific intent as a full defense. That is the intent trap.
wrongExplanations.D: It reaches the correct result but gives the wrong legal reason. The child’s capacity to commit a crime is not the reason Paul is guilty. The reason is Paul’s malicious mental state, shown by reckless firing into shrubs where he believed people might be hiding, and the serious injury that resulted.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: The answer points to trespass and “nondeadly force,” but the call defines the crime as malicious serious injury. It is a partial-defense frame, not the core statutory axis.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: The answer points to Ruth’s criminal responsibility. That is not the actor-malice axis. Correct result, wrong reason.

c3.label: CLASH B vs C
c3.text: B and C fight on one axis: whether “maliciously” requires intent to kill or seriously injure, or whether reckless serious injury can count.

c3.label: CALL / Gold Key
c3.text: Malice can be implied from extreme recklessness. The stem gives recklessness and serious injury. C wins.

studentScript: The call gives the elements: maliciously causing serious physical injury. A talks trespass and nondeadly force; not enough. D talks the child’s criminal responsibility; wrong frame. B and C fight on intent versus recklessness. Gold Key: malice can be reckless. The facts give reckless firing and loss of sight. Pick C.

A.signal: This answer uses trespass and Paul’s belief about nondeadly force, but it does not carry the malice-plus-serious-injury burden.
A.lawyer: Trespass and a belief that force was nondeadly do not automatically defeat liability for maliciously causing serious physical injury.

B.signal: B fights C on one axis: whether malice requires intent or can be recklessness.
B.lawyer: Malice can be implied from gross recklessness; specific intent to kill or cause serious injury is not required.

C.signal: C matches the reckless-firing fact and the serious-injury result.
C.lawyer: Reckless firing into a place where people may be hiding, causing loss of sight, supports malicious serious injury.

D.signal: The charge turns on Paul’s mental state and Ruth’s injury, not Ruth’s criminal responsibility.
D.lawyer: The child-capacity rationale is not the rule that establishes Paul’s guilt.

goldKeys.statement: For a malice offense, do not read 'maliciously' as only 'specifically intended harm.' Malice can be implied from extreme recklessness toward human life or serious injury.
goldKeys.trigger: charged offense uses 'maliciously' and the facts show dangerous reckless firing
goldKeys.unlocks: B's intent-only trap and C's reckless-injury answer
goldKeys.authority: Official row explanation; common-law implied malice / depraved indifference authority

silverKeys.statement: When one answer says 'no intent' and the other says 'reckless injury,' stop and name the axis: intent-only malice vs reckless malice.
silverKeys.trigger: B denies intent; C uses recklessness

remediation.title: Malice is not always intent
remediation.signal: statute says maliciously; answer pair says intent vs recklessness
remediation.studentMove: Name the mental-state axis before choosing.
remediation.trap: Treating no specific intent as automatic acquittal.
